author: garyrong
content: Well, it's more like the implementation details. The EIP just claims that: if the deployment destination has non-empty storage, then reject it. Hardcoding is one cheap way to achieve that

author: garyrong
content: I don't think EIP-7610 will be broken under the EIP-7928.

author: garyrong
content: Originally, Geth implemented this EIP by checking the storage root, which is a more general solution. Unfortunately, the post-transaction storage root is not available in the BAL, and the pre-existing storage root could theoretically be emptied by a preceding transaction. Therefore, relying on the storage root is fragile, within the context of 7928. It's the reason we go with hardcoding approach.

author: taratorio
content: [EIP-8253](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-8253) is a much cleaner solution than hardcoding and furthermore cleans up the mess EIP-7610 introduces. It also cleans up the mess with EELS tests testing for virtually impossible scenarios that now Geth in addition to Reth are not passing.

author: taratorio
content: Geth's hardcoding approach leading to test failures in EELS is an example of EIP-7610 being broken.

author: taratorio
content: We should either 1) take the hardcoding approach and clarify that in EIP-7610 so that tests can be either removed or updated to reflect the hardcode nature of this or 2) we should do EIP-8253
